To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the neutrino factory is superior in terms of systematic uncertainties and statistics to all other proposed long-baseline oscillation experiments.

a neutrino beam with γ ≳ 100 is necessary to achieve the best possible precision on $\deltacps$, that an \spl-based \bbeam with γ =100 is the best possible choice, that a neutrino facility with γ ≲2 is not competitive, and that a neutrino oscillation experiment at a γ ≲2 beam can only be justified if the beam is also used for other experiments such as proton decay searches.

a neutrino beam with an energy of 20–30 GeV, a neutrino factory, and a \bbeam with an energy of about 1 GeV are the only three options that can achieve a precision of $\deltacpm$ ≲ 10$^{\circ}$. The main takeaway from our work is that
the physics case for neutrino factories is compelling, and it should be possible to make a compelling case also for \bbeams and superbeams.

the systematic error in the measurement of \tht₁₃ is not a problem for the measurement of \deltacp, and that the systematic error is not the main reason for the performance gap between a neutrino factory and any other long-baseline neutrinos experiment.

the physics potential of long-baseline oscillation experiments is not limited by the systematic errors in the oscillation analysis, but rather by the precision to which the oscillation parameters can be measured in the first place.
